title: 𒉆𒈗
titleEn: Sumerian King List — Uruk, Ur, Adab, Mari, and the tavern-keeper queen (IV 45 – V 43)
part: Uruk, Ur, Adab, Mari, and the tavern-keeper queen (IV 45 – V 43)
draftNote: Draft — the cuneiform and its readings are provisional, checked sign-by-sign against Langdon's 1923 edition of the prism.
source: Weld-Blundell Prism (WB 444), after S. Langdon, Oxford Editions of Cuneiform Texts II (Oxford, 1923), IV 45 – V 43. Cuneiform in normalized Unicode (Neo-Assyrian forms) though the prism is Old Babylonian. Academic transliteration in modern subscript notation over Langdon's 1923 readings; Langdon's restorations shown in [ ] and his superseded readings flagged in the notes; pronunciation conventional reconstructed Sumerian. Fresh translations from the Sumerian; Langdon's public-domain translation consulted for sense only.
about: The kingship comes back to Uruk for a second dynasty, and then moves quickly through a run of cities: Ur, Adab, Mari, and Kish again. This part covers the foot of Col. IV and most of Col. V. Uruk's second dynasty begins with Enugduanna; then two lines that do not follow the usual pattern give 120 and 480 years without a name. The top of Col. V is broken away for ten lines; Langdon gives the break to a second dynasty of Ur, with four or five names to be supplied. After the break the copy keeps scattered signs: the end of a name, a total for Ur's kings with its numbers lost, and the refrains that send the kingship to Adab (one king, Lugalannimundu, 90 years) and to Mari (six kings, most of their names broken). Then comes Ku-Bau, 'a woman tavern-keeper', 'who made firm the foundation of Kish', the one woman to rule as 'king' in it, for 100 years. The kingship then passes to Akshak. Much of Col. V is Langdon's restoration from other copies; restored words are in brackets, lost numbers are left as gaps, and where his copy shows more (or less) than his transliteration, the copy is followed and the note says so. Some figures do not agree: in IV 48 Langdon's transliteration has 480 years and his translation 420; and Mari's total, 136, leaves 17 years for a reign he restores as 25. These are reported, not corrected. Readings follow Langdon's 1923 edition, signs as his copy of the prism shows them; uncertain signs and names are flagged in the notes.

sentences.i: In Uruk, Enugduanna became king; he reigned 60 years.
sentences.n: The kingship is back in Uruk (IV 44), and its second dynasty opens in the usual way: the city, the king, lugal-am₃, the reign. unug{ki}-ga: Uruk (the UNUG sign + the place-determinative KI; Langdon Unug-(ki)-ga, 'Erech') + -ga, the vowel -a written -ga after the final g of unug; at the head of a dynasty it is the locative 'in', as urim₂{ki}-ma is 'in Ur' (III 39). The king's name is Langdon's En-ū̄g-du-an-na ('Enugduanna'): EN, then a large sign with a long horizontal tail, taken with Langdon as UG, then DU, AN, NA; the identification of the second sign rests on his reading. Langdon (fn. 9, p. 14) says that Poebel's Nippur copy No. 2 had three names here, that En-ug-du-an-na is probably an error for En-šag-kuš-an-na (a ruler known from a Nippur vase inscription), and that the other two are probably Lugal-ki-gub-ni-lăĝ and Lugal-kisal-si; this prism names only one. IV 46: lugal-am₃ (Langdon lugal-ám); '1 šu-ši' — one sixty, with šu-ši 'sixty' written out as a word (Akkadian šūši), as in IV 25 and 40. All signs are clear on the copy (Pl. II).

sentences.n: A line outside the usual pattern. nam-lugal-bi 'its kingship' (nam-lugal + -bi 'its'), then mu '2 šu-ši' — two sixties, 120, with šu-ši written out — and ni-ag, the singular reign verb (ì-aĝ₂, literally 'measured out'), so: '(he) exercised its kingship 120 years'. No name stands with it, and who the 'he' is is not said; Langdon translates impersonally, 'The kingship for 120 years was exercised'. With his fn. 9 (Poebel No. 2 had three names here, this prism one), the line may stand for kings this copy does not name; that is a guess, and the English keeps to what is written. All signs are clear on the copy.

sentences.n: The last line of Col. IV, set in from the left like the totals' lines, and ruled off below. mu, then 480 = 8 geš (8 × 60), drawn 4 over 4 on the copy, then ni-ag: the NI is clear, the AK drawn inside the hatching at the edge of the break (Langdon prints it without brackets). Langdon transliterates 480 but translates 'For 420 years they ruled' — 420 would be 7 geš; the copy has eight wedges, so 480 is shown; the discrepancy is his. His 'they ruled' does not match the singular ni-ag (most totals have ib-ag, though two in this part, V 32 and V 41, also have ni-ag). Whose years these are is not said: there is no name, and the line is not built like a total (no count of kings, no mu-bi). It is rendered literally. Langdon's Introduction (p. 5) takes the figure as the length of the whole dynasty: the scribe 'did not know the names of more than one king here, namely Enugduanna, but knew that the kingdom endured 420 years' — again 420, and his table counts this Uruk dynasty as 1(?) king.

sentences.n: The top of Col. V is broken away: ten lines (V 1–10) are lost entirely (the copy is headed 'Lines 1–10 defaced'; Langdon prints a single row of dots numbered '1-10.'). This one gap unit stands for all ten lines, as Langdon's transliteration and the house conventions treat them as one lost entry. Langdon (Introduction, p. 5) gives the break to a second dynasty of Ur: Poebel's Nippur list (P. No. 2) gives 13 or 14 kings for the three Ur dynasties, the first and third have 9, so he reckons 4 or 5 names to be supplied in the break, with a possible total of 108 years. The second dynasty of Uruk he takes to have ended with IV 48 (one known king, Enugduanna). That it is Ur's kingship that ends here is borne out by the refrain at V 15.

V to survive, and only its last sign: a box with crossing strokes at the right end of the line, read LU by Langdon with his own query ('[. . . . -] LU?'); the reading is uncertain. It is the end of a royal name, the rest lost. V 12: Langdon restores '[mu ? ni- ag]' — the number unknown, so it is shown as a gap. sentences.n: A dynasty's total, over two lines. Langdon prints both lines wholly restored, '[ ? lugal ]' and '[mu-bi ? ib-ag]', with the numbers unknown. His copy shows more: in V 13, LUGAL is drawn in the middle of the line, with hatching before and after it; in V 14, MU and BI stand clear at the start of the line, then hatching, then IB and AK clear at the right end. So lugal, mu-bi and ib-ag are shown here as preserved (the plate decides), and only the two numbers are lost. Which dynasty this total closes depends on the lost lines: by V 15 it is Ur that falls, so this is presumably the total of the dynasty of Ur that followed Uruk in the break.

sentences.i: [Ur was smitten with weapons; its kingship was carried to Adab.]
sentences.n: The refrain, restored entire by Langdon over two lines; on the copy both lines are hatched across their whole width. V 15 '[Uri(ki) ᵍⁱˢku ba-an- sig ]': Ur (ŠEŠ.AB + KI; Langdon Uri) with no case-ending, {ĝeš}tukul 'weapon(s)' (Langdon ᵍⁱˢku), ba-an-sig₃ 'was smitten' (Langdon sig). V 16: Langdon prints '[nam-lugal-bi Adab-(ki)-šú-ba-gín]', with -šú and ba-gín run together by a hyphen — a misprint for '-šú ba-gín'; given here as the refrain has it: nam-lugal-bi 'its kingship', adab{ki}-še₃ 'to Adab' (UD.NUN + KI; -še₃ 'to', Langdon -šú), ba-ĝen 'went' (Langdon ba-gín). Langdon (fn. 1, p. 15) says lines 16 ff. are restored from Legrain, PBS XIII No. 1, V 1 ff. The signs shown are the usual spelling of the restored words; the prism's own are lost.

sentences.i: [In Adab, Lugalannimundu became king; he reigned 90 years.]
sentences.n: The dynasty of Adab: one king. Both lines are wholly restored by Langdon (from Legrain No. 1, fn. 1); the copy is hatched across them. V 17 '[Adab-(ki)-a Lugal-an-ni-mu-un-dū]': adab{ki}-a 'in Adab' (UD.NUN + KI + the locative -a), and the name Lugalannimundu (Langdon's English 'Lugalannimundu'): lugal 'king' + an-ni (perhaps An with the ergative -e) + mu-un-du₃ 'he built', the last written with the KAK sign (Langdon dū, read du₃ 'build' by sign). No -a closes the verb, so it is not a relative clause ('whom … built'); how the parts go together is uncertain, and the name is given as a name. V 18 '[lugal-ám mu 90 ni- ag]': lugal-am₃ 'was king', 90 = 1 geš + 3 u (60 + 30), ni-ag 'he ruled'.

sentences.n: The total for Adab, over two lines. V 19: the count is restored ('[1 ]'), lugal is clear on the copy at the right of the line. V 20: '[mu-bi 90] ib-ag' — IB and AK are clear; just before them, at the edge of the hatching, the copy draws a trace (a corner-wedge), perhaps the last u of the 90, which Langdon nevertheless prints inside his brackets. 90 = 1 geš + 3 u, the same as the reign. Langdon (fn. 2, p. 15) adds that the local records of Adab mention two more kings, Mebasi and Lugaldalu.

sentences.i: Adab was smitten with weapons; its kingship was carried to Mari.
sentences.n: The refrain, over two lines. V 21: Adab is in the break ('[Adab-(ki)]'); then GIŠ, KU, BA, AN and the compact verb-sign are clear on the copy: {ĝeš}tukul ba-an-sig₃. Langdon prints 'ka-an- sig' — a misprint: the copy's sign is BA, drawn as in the same refrain at IV 36 and IV 43, and his translation has 'was smitten'. V 22: '[nam-lugal-bi] Ma-er-(ki)-šú ba-gín': a trace at the edge of the hatching (perhaps the end of BI), then MA, a second sign, KI, EŠ₂, BA, DU, all clear. Langdon reads the city Ma-er ('Maer'); the second sign is drawn like the URU of III 15 (a box with an inner upright and cross-stroke), not like the IR of III 27, so it is given here as URU, read ri₂ by sign — ma-ri₂{ki}, Mari. The identification is the drafter's, from the copy; Langdon's 'er' is the reading he gives. -še₃ 'to' (Langdon -šú), ba-ĝen 'went' (Langdon ba-gín).

sentences.i: In Mari, Ansir became king; he reigned 30 years.
sentences.n: The dynasty of Mari opens. V 23 '[Ma-er-ki]-šú An-sir': the city is in the break, but EŠ₂ (-še₃) is drawn at its edge, so the prism wrote 'to Mari' where the opening formula has the locative 'in' (Langdon, fn. 3, notes that Legrain No. 1 V 10 has Ma-er-(ki)-a, 'in Mari'); the English follows the formula and the literal line marks the oddity. The king is An-sir (Langdon 'Ansir'): AN, then a sign drawn like the BU of IV 26 (two wedges and a long horizontal), which Langdon reads sir; by sign it is BU read sir₂. Langdon (fn. 4) gives 'An-bu' and 'An-sud' as possible: both are other readings of the same BU sign, so the name's reading is uncertain. V 24 '[lugal-ám] mu 30 ni-ag': lugal-am₃ in the break; mu, 30 = 3 u, and ni-ag clear.

sentences.i: Lugaltarzi, son of Ansir, reigned […] years.
sentences.n: Langdon '[Lugal-tar-]zi dumu An-sir- ge', with zi outside his brackets. On the copy the line is hatched up to a sign that is drawn exactly like the TUR (dumu) of III 43; then AN, the BU sign (sir₂) and KID are clear. So zi too is in the break, and the whole name is shown as restored. dumu an-sir₂-ke₄ 'son of Ansir': -ke₄ (KID; Langdon -ge) is the genitive -ak 'of' + the ergative -e, marking 'son of X' as the subject. V 26: Langdon '[mu- 25 (?) ] ni- ag' — the number restored with his own query, 'from the total in l. 32' (fn. 5); per house rule a doubtful restoration is not shown as signs, so the number is a gap. His 25 does not agree with that total as the copy gives it: the total is 136 (V 32), and the five surviving reigns of Mari (30 + 30 + 20 + 30 + 9) make 119, which would leave 17 for Lugaltarzi; with 25 the sum is 144. NI and AK are clear.

sentences.n: The total for Mari, over two lines. V 31: 6 diš, lugal. V 32: mu-bi is in the break (Langdon '[mu-bi ]'); then 136, which Langdon writes '120 + 16': 2 geš (120) + 1 u + 6 diš (16). The verb is ni-ag, the singular of the single reigns, not ib-ag as in the other totals; the literal line keeps it, the English follows the sense. The total does not add up to the reigns as they survive: 30 (Ansir) + a lost figure (Lugaltarzi) + 30 + 20 + 30 + 9 = 119 plus the lost one, so 17 years would be left for Lugaltarzi, not the 25 Langdon restores in V 26 (with 25 the reigns make 144). Reported, not corrected.

sentences.i: In Kish, Ku-Bau, a woman tavern-keeper, who made firm the foundation of Kish, became king; she reigned 100 years.
sentences.n: The third dynasty of Kish: one ruler, a woman. Four lines, the left half of each in the break. V 36 '[Kiš-(ki) Kug-ᵈ]Baú': Kish restored, then the name Ku-Bau: ku₃ 'pure, holy' (KU₃; Langdon kug) + the divine determinative + the goddess Bau (BA + U₂; Langdon Baú). BA is half in the hatching, U₂ clear. V 37 '[munuz-galu-kaš-tin-]na': restored except NA; a trace of the sign before NA shows at the edge of the break. munus 'woman' (the SAL sign; Langdon munuz), lu₂ 'person' (Langdon galu), kaš 'beer' (KAŠ = BI×A), tin (DIN), -na: lu₂ kaš-tin-na, word by word 'person of kaš-tin', Langdon 'a female wine seller', i.e. a woman who keeps a drinking-house — a tavern-keeper. What tin adds (it also writes 'wine' in geštin, and 'life') and the exact analysis of -na (the -a 'of' after n?) are uncertain; the restoration itself comes from another copy (fn. 1). V 38 '[suĝuš Kiš-(ki)] mu-un-gi-na': suḫuš 'foundation' (Langdon suĝuš) and kiš are in the break, but KI is drawn at its edge, then MU, UN, GI, NA clear: mu-un-gi-na 'made firm' (gi-n with mu-n- and the -a of a 'who' clause, as Etana's kur-kur mu-un-gi-na, II 18). V 39 '[lugal-]ám mu 100 ni-ag': lugal in the break, the A at its edge, AN clear (am₃ = A.AN); 100 = 1 geš + 4 u. She is called lugal 'king' like the men; ni-ag is the same 3sg verb ('she ruled').

morph.gloss: one
king
'its years' — mu 'years' + -bi 'its'
60 (the base of the system)
ì-aĝ₂ (Langdon 'ni-ag') — 'he ruled', lit. 'measured out'; reign verb, 3sg

sentences.n: The total for the third dynasty of Kish, over two lines, all clear: 1 diš, lugal; mu-bi, 100 = 1 geš + 4 u, the same as Ku-Bau's reign. Here again (as at V 32) the total has ni-ag, the singular, not ib-ag; the house literal keeps 'he-ruled', the English follows the sense. lugal 'king' is used of the woman too.

sentences.l: Kish with-weapons was-smitten; its-kingship, Akshak, was-established.

morph.gloss: Kish — city in northern Babylonia, seat of the first dynasty after the Flood (KIŠ + place-det ki)
wood determinative (ĝeš) — marks a wooden object
weapon, mace (the KU sign with ĝeš; Langdon ᵍⁱˢku)
ba-n- — verbal prefix chain (ba- often gives a passive sense)
to strike, smite (written PA.GAN₂; Langdon sīg)
kingship
'its / that' (3rd-person possessive)
Akšak (Langdon Akšak) — city in northern Babylonia; written UD.KUŠU₂ (as identified here) plus the place-determinative KI, as akšak{ki}; the identification of the signs is not certain
ba-gub — 'was set up, established' (gub written with the DU sign)

sentences.i: Kish was smitten with weapons; its kingship was established at Akshak.
sentences.n: The refrain, over two lines, all clear on the copy. V 42 'Kiš-ki ᵍⁱˢku ba- an- sig': kiš{ki} {ĝeš}tukul ba-an-sig₃. V 43 'nam-lugal-bi Akšak-(ki) ba-gub': nam-lugal-bi 'its kingship', then the city Akšak: two signs before KI, taken as the conventional writing UD.KUŠU₂ (the copy's forms are not distinct enough to confirm the second sign; the identification is uncertain), with no -še₃ 'to' written, and the verb is ba-gub (gub 'to stand, set up', the DU sign), not ba-ĝen 'went': literally 'its kingship, Akšak, was set up'. Langdon: 'The rulership at Akšak was established'. The English follows the published rendering of the same ba-gub at Larak and Shuruppak in Col. I: 'its kingship was established at …'. Langdon (fn. 6) says that here begins the Scheil Dynastic Tablet (BM 108857).

glossary.-a: nominalizer · locative -a 'in, at' on a city name (adab{ki}-a 'in Adab')
glossary.-am₃: enclitic copula 'is / was' — written am₃ = a-an
glossary.-ga: genitive -a(k) 'of', written -ga after a final g (unug{ki}-ga 'of Uruk') · locative -a 'in, at', likewise written -ga after a final g (unug{ki}-ga 'in Uruk', at the head of a dynasty)
glossary.-ke₄: genitive -ak 'of' + ergative -e, written with the KID sign (Langdon -ge) — marks a genitive phrase such as 'son of X' as the subject (agent) of the verb; not always written
glossary.-na: -a(k) 'of' (genitive) written -na after a final n, as in lu₂ kaš-tin-na 'person of kaš-tin'; the analysis is uncertain
glossary.-šú: terminative -šè/-šú — 'to, towards' (the EŠ₂ sign) · also written where the formula has the locative -a 'in' (ma-ri₂{ki}-še₃ at the head of a dynasty, where another copy has ma-ri₂{ki}-a); why the terminative stands there is uncertain
glossary.[…]: a lost stretch of text — a gap where the signs are broken away on the prism
glossary.[…]-bi: […]-bi (Langdon '. . . -bi') — king of Mari; only the end of the name survives and the rest is lost
glossary.[…]-bi-im: […]-bim (Langdon '. . . bi-im') — king of Mari; only the end of the name survives and the rest is lost
glossary.[…]-lu: […]-lu — the end of a royal name; only a final sign survives, which Langdon reads LU with a query, and the rest is lost; nothing more can be said of the name
glossary.[…]-lugal: […]-lugal — king of Mari; only the end of the name survives and the rest is lost
glossary.[…]-lu₂-gal: […]-lugal (Langdon '. . . lù-gal') — king of Mari; only the end of the name survives, written lu₂-gal; the rest is lost
glossary.adab: Adab (Langdon Adab) — city in central Babylonia; written UD.NUN plus the place-determinative KI, as adab{ki}
glossary.akšak: Akšak (Langdon Akšak) — city in northern Babylonia; written UD.KUŠU₂ (as identified here) plus the place-determinative KI, as akšak{ki}; the identification of the signs is not certain
glossary.an-sir₂: Ansir (Langdon An-sir) — first king of Mari; AN + the BU sign, whose readings bu, sir₂, sud leave the name uncertain (Langdon also allows An-bu and An-sud)
glossary.ba-an-: ba-n- — verbal prefix chain: ba- (often of motion away, or a middle/passive sense) + -n-, which ordinarily marks a 'he' who acts · in intransitive verbs of motion (ba-an-ku₄ 'entered') the -n- has no clear 'he' to mark; its function there is uncertain
glossary.ba-gub: ba-gub — 'was set up, established' (gub written with the DU sign)
glossary.ba-gín: ba-ĝen — 'went, passed' (ĝen written with the DU sign)
glossary.dumu: son, child — written with the TUR sign, read dumu; 'dumu X' = 'son of X'
glossary.en-ug-du-an-na: Enugduanna (Langdon En-ū̄g-du-an-na) — first king of the second dynasty of Uruk; EN + a sign read UG after Langdon (the identification is his and uncertain) + DU-AN-NA; Langdon thinks the name may be an error for En-šag-kuš-an-na, a ruler known from another source
glossary.gi-n: to make firm, establish — gi-n 'firm, true'; Langdon 'make faithful'
glossary.kaš-tin: kaš-tin — a compound of kaš 'beer' (written with the sign BI×A) and tin (DIN); in lu₂ kaš-tin-na Langdon takes it as 'wine seller' (the tavern-keeper); what tin adds to kaš is uncertain
glossary.kiš: Kish — city in northern Babylonia, seat of the first dynasty after the Flood; written with the KIŠ sign plus the place-determinative KI (unread), as kiš{ki} · the kingship returns to it more than once, so it is also the seat of later dynasties of Kish
glossary.ku₃-{d}ba-u₂: Ku-Bau (Langdon Kug-ᵈBaú) — the one ruler of the third dynasty of Kish, a woman; ku₃ 'pure, holy' + the goddess Bau (BA-U₂), with the divine determinative
glossary.lugal-an-ni-mu-un-du₃: Lugalannimundu (Langdon Lugal-an-ni-mu-un-dū) — the one king of Adab; the name is not preserved on this prism and is restored by Langdon from another copy; the last sign is KAK, read du₃ by sign; the sense of the name is uncertain
glossary.lugal-tar-zi: Lugaltarzi (Langdon [Lugal-tar-]zi) — king of Mari, son of Ansir; the name is in the break on this copy and is restored by Langdon; lugal 'king' + tar + zi, the sense of the name uncertain
glossary.lu₂: man; 'the one who …' — introduces a relative ('who') clause; Langdon galu
glossary.ma-ri₂: Mari (Langdon Ma-er) — city on the middle Euphrates; MA + a second sign drawn like URU, read ri₂ by sign (Langdon er), plus the place-determinative KI, as ma-ri₂{ki}; the second sign is identified from the copy
glossary.mu-un-: mu-n- — verbal prefix chain: mu- + -n- 'he' (the doer)
glossary.munus: woman, female — the SAL sign (Langdon munuz)
glossary.ni-ag: ì-aĝ₂ (Langdon 'ni-ag') — 'he ruled', lit. 'measured out'; reign verb, 3sg
glossary.sig₃: to strike, smite — written as one compact sign taken as PA.GAN₂ (Langdon sīg, also printed sig); the identification of the drawn form is uncertain
glossary.suḫuš: foundation, base — the SUḪUŠ sign (Langdon suĝuš)
glossary.tukul: weapon, mace — the KU sign with the wood determinative ĝeš (Langdon ᵍⁱˢku)
glossary.unug: Uruk (Langdon Unug, Erech) — city in southern Babylonia, the seat of this dynasty; written with the UNUG sign (AB-gunû) plus the place-determinative KI (unread), as unug{ki}
glossary.urim₂: Ur — city in southern Babylonia (written ŠEŠ.AB plus place-determinative KI, as urim₂{ki}; Langdon Uri)
glossary.{d}: divine determinative (diĝir) — marks the following name as a god
glossary.{ĝeš}: wood determinative (ĝeš, the GIŠ sign) — unread, marks a wooden object; Langdon writes it as a raised ᵍⁱˢ
glossary.šu-ši: šu-ši — 'sixty', written out as a word (Akkadian šūši) instead of with a numeral sign
